brave.title: Yesterday's News, Today's "Newly Acquired Information" -- The First Circuit's CBE Time Warp | Drug & Device Law
brave.snippet:
Here is a question the First Circuit has now answered the wrong way — can a scientific paper published before the FDA approved a drug nonetheless qualify as “newly acquired information” that triggers a duty to change the warnings under the Changes Being Effected regulation? The Fifth Circuit said no last year in Hickey. The Fourth Circuit said no in Knight. The First Circuit’s own prior panel in Celexa said no. And now, in Warner v. Amgen Inc., — F.4th —-, 2026 WL 3033704 (1st Cir.
Warner is a hard case. A young man with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease died at twenty-five from cerebrovascular complications after taking a single dose of Aimovig, the defendant’s CGRP-receptor antagonist for migraine prevention. Id. at *1. There is no way to write about this one lightly, and we’re not going to try. But the law does not change because the facts are tragic, and the law the First Circuit announced here is, at least in part, a problem.
And here is the awkward part for the First Circuit — it had already said the same thing. In In re Celexa & Lexapro Marketing & Sales Practices Litigation, 779 F.3d 34, 41 (1st Cir. 2015) — which the Warner panel itself quotes — the court explained that the “newly acquired information” requirement “lets the FDA be the exclusive judge of safety and efficacy based on information available at the commencement of marketing, while allowing the states to reach contrary conclusions when new information not considered by the FDA develops.” Warner, 2026 WL 3033704, at *10 (quoting Celexa) (emphasis added).
The Fourth Circuit in Knight and the Fifth Circuit in Hickey — and, before them, the First Circuit’s own panel in Celexa — had put the field on reasonably firm ground that information already in the FDA’s hands (or in the public scientific literature) at the time of approval is not “newly acquired” when a plaintiff later rediscovers it. Warner nudges that ground.

ceramic.snippet:
A federal district court in Massachusetts dismissed a wrongful death suit brought by the estate of a young man who passed away alleging that Amgen Inc. and Amgen USA Inc. failed to provide adequate warnings on its injectable migraine medicine Aimovig. The court dismissed the suit, finding that the estate’s claims were preempted to the extent they alleged that Amgen had a state-law duty to submit a stronger warning label to the FDA in its pre-approval review of Aimovig. The estate argued that Amgen’s warnings should have included that individuals with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease or surgery were excluded from the clinical testing done to obtain FDA approval. The estate asserted that its claims were not preempted by the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), because the drug maker could have included such a warning pre-approval in its new drug application or defendant could have changed the warning post-approval under the Changes Being Effected (CBE) regulations. The court disagreed and found the pre- and post-approval failure to warn claims were preempted (  Warner v. Amgen Inc. , No. 1:24-cv-10632-JEK (D. Mass. Feb. 13, 2025)).

   Preemption. The court began its analysis by noting that it did not even need to look at whether or not Massachusetts law requires such warnings, as the estate’s wrongful death claim was preempted by the FDCA under Supreme Court and First Circuit precedent. Wrote the court, “Insofar as [the estate] seeks to hold Amgen liable for failing to propose a stronger warning label to the FDA before Aimovig’s approval, [the] claim is preempted because the FDA considered the exclusion criteria used in Aimovig’s clinical trials and the theoretical risks associated with CGRP antagonism.

# Justia Drugs & Biotech Opinion Summaries
Lucas Warner, a young man with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease, died after taking a single dose of Aimovig, a biologic drug manufactured by Amgen and approved by the FDA to prevent migraines.

After Warner filed a wrongful death claim in Massachusetts state court, Amgen removed the case to the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Amgen moved to dismiss the complaint, arguing federal law preempted Warner’s state law claims because Amgen was required to use the FDA-approved label and Warner had not shown Amgen could have unilaterally changed it. At the hearing, Warner sought leave to amend her complaint, alleging newly available studies could have permitted Amgen to update the label using FDA’s Changes Being Effected (CBE) procedure.

The district court dismissed the complaint as preempted and denied leave to amend, finding the studies insufficient and the amendment futile.The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reviewed the case. It affirmed the dismissal of Warner’s original complaint, holding that federal law preempted the claim because Amgen could not unilaterally alter the label during FDA approval, and the FDA would have rejected Warner’s proposed label changes.

The case was remanded for further proceedings limited to Warner’s claims based on this post-approval labeling theory.

The company appealed.The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reviewed the case de novo.

This is a wrongful death action brought by plaintiff Elissa Warner, as the personal
representative of the Estate of Lucas Warner, against defendants Amgen Inc. and Amgen USA
Inc. (collectively “Amgen”).

Warner contends that Amgen’s labeling for Aimovig failed to provide adequate warnings
that individuals with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease or surgery, like Lucas, were
excluded from the FDA’s clinical testing for Aimovig. After removing the case to this Court,
Amgen now moves to dismiss Warner’s complaint for failure to state a claim. Amgen contends
that Warner’s wrongful death claim is preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,
21 U.S.C. § 301 et seq., because it would have been impossible to comply with federal regulations
governing prescription drug labeling and any state-law duty to provide warnings beyond those
already included in Aimovig’s label.
Agreeing with Amgen, the Court will grant the motion to dismiss and deny Warner’s
request for leave to amend the complaint. Under First Circuit precedent, Warner’s claims are
preempted to the extent they allege that Amgen had a state-law duty to submit a stronger warning
label to the FDA in its pre-approval review of Aimovig. And even accounting for the studies that
Warner submits in connection with her request for leave to amend, Amgen has established that no
newly acquired information came to light in the month between Aimovig’s approval and Lucas’s
injection that would have permitted Amgen to unilaterally change Aimovig’s label under the
FDA’s “changes being effected” regulation.

First Circuit Revives Aimovig Wrongful-Death Suit Against Amgen Over Label Change

The court held that four scientific articles not shown to have reached the FDA could plausibly have let Amgen add a brain-injury warning to Aimovig after approval.
By LitNews Newsroom Oct 10, 2026

Key Points

* The First Circuit held that a state-law claim faulting the label a manufacturer proposed in its biologics license application is preempted, because that application is a request for FDA approval rather than a unilateral act.
* The court independently held that the FDA knew Aimovig's trials excluded patients with seizure and neurological histories, considered a cerebrovascular warning, and rejected it, so a request for Warner's proposed label would have been denied.
* The court reversed the denial of leave to amend, holding that the Rehni, Liu, Sorby-Adams and Zhai articles plausibly qualify as newly acquired information supporting a post-approval label change under 21 C.F.R. § 601.12(f)(2).
* The court declined to exclude animal studies that did not test Aimovig, noting that the FDA itself relied on such studies, and held that a study published before approval can be newly acquired if it was never submitted to the FDA.
* Amgen did not rely on a 'clear evidence' defense that the FDA would have rejected the change anyway, and the court left that reserved defense unaddressed on remand.

Elissa E. Warner v. Amgen Inc.

October 9, 2026 · 25-1268 · Panel Decision · Kayatta · By James Taylor
The First Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a wrongful death claim regarding the drug Aimovig but reversed the denial of leave to amend the complaint to allege failure to warn based on newly acquired information.
Listen to this decision 0:00 / 0:56
Download
Report a problem with this audio

Key takeaways

* Holding: Affirmed in part and remanded in part.
* Standard: De novo review of dismissal and denial of leave to amend.
* Vote: Panel Decision
* Practical effect: Manufacturers may face liability for failing to update labels with newly acquired safety information even after initial FDA approval, provided they could have done so under the Changes Being Effected regulation.

Background

Elissa Warner sued Amgen Inc. after her son Lucas died from cerebrovascular complications following a single dose of Aimovig, a biologic drug for migraine prevention. The district court dismissed the complaint, ruling the claims were preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and denied leave to amend the complaint to allege that Amgen should have updated the label after approval but before the death.

The court’s reasoning

The court explained that while the original complaint was preempted because it challenged the FDA-approved label, the district court erred in denying leave to amend. The amendment sought to allege that Amgen failed to use the Changes Being Effected regulation to update the label based on newly acquired information, which is not necessarily preempted.

What it means going forward

Manufacturers may face liability for failing to update labels with newly acquired safety information even after initial FDA approval, provided they could have done so under the Changes Being Effected regulation.

Amgen Inc*, 2026 WL 3033704 (1st Cir. October 9, 2026).
The First Circuit (Montecalvo, Lipez, Kayatta) affirmed the dismissal of a failure-to-warn suit against a pharmaceutical manufacturer but remanded for the plaintiff to amend her complaint.
The plaintiff’s theory of liability was preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act based on impossibility preemption.
The FDCA requires Food and Drug Administration approval of biologic-product labels; the fact that Amgen could have requested a change to its label doesn’t defeat preemption, because FDA would have had to approve it.
Moreover, the record here establishes that FDA would have rejected the change in question.
However, an alternative theory of liability that the plaintiff presented—that, based on newly acquired information, Amgen should have used a statutory procedure to supplement its label post-approval—was not clearly preempted and thus not futile, and the district court should have granted leave to amend.

Amgen Inc*, 2026 WL 3033704 (1st Cir. October 9, 2026).
The First Circuit (Montecalvo, Lipez, Kayatta) affirmed the dismissal of a failure-to-warn suit against a pharmaceutical manufacturer but remanded for the plaintiff to amend her complaint.
The plaintiff’s theory of liability was preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act based on impossibility preemption.
The FDCA requires Food and Drug Administration approval of biologic-product labels; the fact that Amgen could have requested a change to its label doesn’t defeat preemption, because FDA would have had to approve it.
Moreover, the record here establishes that FDA would have rejected the change in question.
However, an alternative theory of liability that the plaintiff presented—that, based on newly acquired information, Amgen should have used a statutory procedure to supplement its label post-approval—was not clearly preempted and thus not futile, and the district court should have granted leave to amend.

seltz.snippet:
Here is a question the First Circuit has now answered the wrong way — can a scientific paper published *before* the FDA approved a drug nonetheless qualify as “newly acquired information” that triggers a duty to change the warnings under the Changes Being Effected regulation? The Fifth Circuit said no last year in *Hickey*. The Fourth Circuit said no in *Knight*. The First Circuit’s own prior panel in *Celexa* said no. And now, in *Warner v. Amgen Inc.*, — F.4th —-, 2026 WL 3033704 (1st Cir. Oct. 9, 2026), the First Circuit has said — maybe yes.

*Warner* is a hard case. A young man with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease died at twenty-five from cerebrovascular complications after taking a single dose of Aimovig, the defendant’s CGRP-receptor antagonist for migraine prevention. *Id.* at *1. There is no way to write about this one lightly, and we’re not going to try. But the law does not change because the facts are tragic, and the law the First Circuit announced here is, at least in part, a problem.

This is a wrongful death action brought by plaintiff Elissa Warner, as the personal
representative of the Estate of Lucas Warner, against defendants Amgen Inc. and Amgen USA
Inc. (collectively “Amgen”).

Warner contends that Amgen’s labeling for Aimovig failed to provide adequate warnings
that individuals with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease or surgery, like Lucas, were
excluded from the FDA’s clinical testing for Aimovig. After removing the case to this Court,
Amgen now moves to dismiss Warner’s complaint for failure to state a claim. Amgen contends
that Warner’s wrongful death claim is preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,
21 U.S.C. § 301 et seq., because it would have been impossible to comply with federal regulations
governing prescription drug labeling and any state-law duty to provide warnings beyond those
already included in Aimovig’s label.
Agreeing with Amgen, the Court will grant the motion to dismiss and deny Warner’s
request for leave to amend the complaint. Under First Circuit precedent, Warner’s claims are
preempted to the extent they allege that Amgen had a state-law duty to submit a stronger warning
label to the FDA in its pre-approval review of Aimovig. And even accounting for the studies that
Warner submits in connection with her request for leave to amend, Amgen has established that no
newly acquired information came to light in the month between Aimovig’s approval and Lucas’s
injection that would have permitted Amgen to unilaterally change Aimovig’s label under the
FDA’s “changes being effected” regulation.

For the foregoing reasons, Amgen’s motion to dismiss, ECF 12, is GRANTED. The
complaint is DISMISSED with prejudice and without leave to amend.

October 9, 2026 KAYATTA, Circuit Judge. This appeal arises out of a wrongful death suit concerning the prescription medication Aimovig, a biologic manufactured by Amgen Inc. and Amgen U.S.A. Inc. (collectively, "Amgen") for the prevention of migraines. Lucas Warner, who had a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease, died at the age of twenty-five from cerebrovascular complications after taking a single dose of Aimovig.
Warner v. Amgen Inc. — Brought to you by Free Law Project, a non-profit dedicated to creating high quality open legal information.
At the motion hearing for Amgen's motion to dismiss, Warner introduced a new contention. In addition to critiquing Amgen's efforts to secure FDA approval of the label in the first instance, she contended that a series of studies and literature reviews not known to the FDA during the approval process would have allowed Amgen to employ the CBE procedure to change the label after it was approved and before Lucas took the drug.

you.title: Yesterday's News, Today's "Newly Acquired Information" -- The First ...
you.snippet:
Here is a question the First Circuit has now answered the wrong way — can a scientific paper published before the FDA approved a drug nonetheless qualify as “newly acquired information” that triggers a duty to change the warnings under the Changes Being Effected regulation? The Fifth Circuit said no last year in Hickey. The Fourth Circuit said no in Knight. The First Circuit’s own prior panel in Celexa said no. And now, in Warner v. Amgen Inc., — F.4th —-, 2026 WL 3033704 (1st Cir.
Warner is a hard case. A young man with a history of seizures and cerebrovascular disease died at twenty-five from cerebrovascular complications after taking a single dose of Aimovig, the defendant’s CGRP-receptor antagonist for migraine prevention. Id. at *1. There is no way to write about this one lightly, and we’re not going to try. But the law does not change because the facts are tragic, and the law the First Circuit announced here is, at least in part, a problem.
And here is the awkward part for the First Circuit — it had already said the same thing. In In re Celexa & Lexapro Marketing & Sales Practices Litigation, 779 F.3d 34, 41 (1st Cir. 2015) — which the Warner panel itself quotes — the court explained that the “newly acquired information” requirement “lets the FDA be the exclusive judge of safety and efficacy based on information available at the commencement of marketing, while allowing the states to reach contrary conclusions when new information not considered by the FDA develops.” Warner, 2026 WL 3033704, at *10 (quoting Celexa) (emphasis added).
The Fourth Circuit in Knight and the Fifth Circuit in Hickey — and, before them, the First Circuit’s own panel in Celexa — had put the field on reasonably firm ground that information already in the FDA’s hands (or in the public scientific literature) at the time of approval is not “newly acquired” when a plaintiff later rediscovers it. Warner nudges that ground.
